notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0057.tlg052.1st1K-gr: The heading's ΠΙΠΟΚΡΑΤΕΙ is read as ΙΠΠΟΚΡΑΤΕΙ. Κῶμα and its derivatives are kept as 'coma' and 'comatose' because the meaning of the word is what the essay debates; the sense is not the modern clinical one. Καταφορά is rendered 'lapse' throughout. In 1.5, the sentence ending μήτε σφάλμα τι, μήτ' ἄγνοιαν μηδεμίαν ὑποστέλλεσθαι is obscure and the sense of ὑποστέλλεσθαι uncertain; the text may be corrupt. In 2.1, the parenthesis (ἀπιότ. καὶ ἀχειρόπ.) is abbreviated and unintelligible as it stands, probably a misplaced marginal or printed insertion, so it is transliterated and not translated. Also in 2.1, ὅτι μετὰ πυρετοῦ is read as ὅ τι ('whatever'), and the construction τὸ δ', ὅταν ... εἴπῃ is loose and has been rendered 'And then, when ...'. 'The Artemisium' is the temple of Artemis on Thasos. The Homeric lines are Odyssey 18.201 and Iliad 14.359.

Line 3.1: 'οὔτε γὰρ χωρὶς φράζουσί τι καὶ πανούργως' is defective, with something apparently lost after χωρὶς (the printed text has a break marker there); the rendering is literal and the sense is uncertain, and πανούργως ('craftily') may be corrupt. 'ἀκούειν προθυμότατοί' ('most eager to listen') is odd in a description of violent patients and may be corrupt. 'πρόχειρον' of breathing is rendered 'quick', but the sense is uncertain. 'μετὰ γάρ τινων' ('with some [words]') is unclear and may be corrupt. 'μεδεμιᾶς' is read as μηδεμιᾶς. The verb παρέκοψε is hard to distinguish from its neighbours in the list; 'went off course' is tentative. The argument distinguishes two particles written alike here: interrogative ἆρα (doubt) and inferential ἄρα; the printed accents do not always keep them apart, and the word is left as *ara* where the point depends on it. Galen calls it both adverb and conjunction. σύναγμα in the Epidemics VI quotation is rendered 'contraction', but the sense is uncertain. Archecrates, a patient named in the Prorrhetic quotation, is not otherwise identified. Line 4.1: the final sentence seems incomplete or corrupt ('καὶ ἄλλως διὰ τοῦ εἰσίν…'), and the stretch ends with its point unresolved. 'ἐκείνῳ' is taken to refer to the mixed affection.

nodes.text: GALEN'S BOOK ON COMA IN HIPPOCRATES.

What on earth does the word 'coma' mean in Hippocrates? Is it the lapse into sleep, as some of the commentators have said? Or sleep itself? Or, as others [say], the sleepy lapse? For some have used this name too, making their explanation with a compound designation. Others, however, say that none of these, but the lethargic lapse is what the man calls coma. From the other ancient writers no testimony of any great weight could be had: for even if they apply the word above all to a different thing, nothing prevents Hippocrates from using it differently. For instance, in the poet the word would seem to denote sleep:
'Truly, a soft coma covered me in my dreadful suffering.'
'— — since I covered him round with soft coma.'

But Hippocrates plainly does not use it in this way, if indeed he says that coma often occurs along with sleeplessness and accompanies phrenitics. At the beginning of the *Prorrhetic* he writes the following: 'Those who become comatose at the beginning, with pain of the head, loin, hypochondrium and neck, and who are sleepless: are they perhaps phrenitic?' And in the third book of the *Epidemics* (let us take our testimonies from some of the books agreed to be genuinely his) he says something like this: 'On the eleventh [day] he was in his senses, but he was comatose; urine abundant, thin and black; sleepless.' Then next he says this: 'In this woman the urine was throughout black, thin and watery, and coma accompanied; without appetite, sleepless, despondent.' For in all the passages cited he plainly mentions both sleeplessness and coma. And again, describing another patient in the same book, he says: 'In this man throughout, from the time I too knew of it, the bowel was disturbed, urine thin and black, comatose, sleepless.' So it is directly clear that in him the word 'coma' denotes neither sleep nor lapse. For this reason, I suppose, some of the commentators say that the comatose were named from *kōmazein* [to go reveling]: for those who revel are awake, and the comatose too are awake. And, by Zeus, just as revelers do not nod downward very much, so neither [do] those in coma, and especially with their eyes. For [they say] these are moist, red, unsteady and sunken; but in both groups the whole body is unstable in its movements and without control; and for this reason Hippocrates himself is at a loss about the whole syndrome, whether one should call them phrenitics or something else. For [they say] he is wary of calling them phrenitics, since they are not yet delirious; but, seeing all the phrenitic symptoms, since the patient has pain in the head, loin, hypochondrium and neck, he shrinks from neither any slip nor any ignorance. That this is not plausible no one would argue; yet it does not seem to me at least to have been said adequately, or with demonstration. For the explanation of the expression should have been made from Hippocrates himself, so that we could say not only that it was stated plausibly, but also that it accords with his thinking. For I do not think that the good commentator should consider only this, whether he has spoken plausibly or truly, but also whether he keeps to the thinking of the author, which was not [done] in the foregoing account; although part of the old writer's thinking about the word has been shown through the passages in which he appeared to recognize coma as sleeplessness. And perhaps someone might think he already has the whole of it; but if he waits a little and hears other passages from the same book, the third of the *Epidemics*, he will find that he knows, far from the whole, not even half of the whole.

Consider, then, what he says about a certain woman patient: 'Another woman, the wife of a household slave, after a miscarriage at about the fifth month, was seized by fever; at the beginning she was comatose, and then again sleepless.' For he plainly distinguishes coma from sleeplessness by antithesis, as opposites. And again in the pestilential constitution he says: 'Comatose for much of the time, and then again sleepless.' And a little later: 'The phrenitics and those with burning fever were especially comatose. But also in the other diseases, the most severe, whatever occurred with fever. Throughout, in most cases, either heavy coma accompanied, or they slept thin and small sleeps.' And again: 'In Thasos the man from Paros, who lay above the Artemisium, was seized by acute fever, at first continuous, burning, thirsty; at the beginning comatose, and then again sleepless.' For in all these he sets sleeplessness in antithesis to coma. It is, at any rate, his habit to express himself in this way: you will find him ten thousand times, whenever he mentions opposite things, writing in this manner, or rather never otherwise, as I shall set down a few of many instances from the same book. For it seems better to take all the examples from one [book]. Recording two women before the pestilential constitution, of the first he says: 'Another woman, the wife of a household slave, after a miscarriage at about the fifth month, was seized by fever; at the beginning she was comatose, and then again sleepless.' And of the second he says: 'A woman who lay at the Liars' Market, having then given birth for the first time, with difficulty, to a male child, was seized by fever; and again toward night she had a further shivering fit, her extremities did not warm up, she did not sleep, she was slightly deranged, and then again quickly was in her senses; on the eighth, about midday, she became warm, thirsty, comatose, nauseated.' Next, in [the account of] the pestilence, he describes many patients, and first of all the one I mentioned a little earlier, who was ill in a varied and irregular way, and underwent many changes, often, to the opposite (*apiot.* and *acheirop.*). He begins in this way: 'In Thasos the man from Paros, who lay above the Artemisium, was seized by acute fever.' But for the present argument there is no need of the first days; I shall mention those I need. 'On the eleventh he sweated, not all over; he became chilled, but quickly grew warm again.' For 'grew warm' would clearly be the opposite of 'became chilled'. Then: 'On the twelfth, acute fever; stools bilious, thin, copious; suspended matter in the urine; he was deranged. On the seventeenth, painfully: for there was no sleep, and the fever intensified. On the twentieth he sweated all over, without fever; stools bilious; without appetite, comatose. On the twenty-fourth he relapsed. On the thirty-fourth, without fever; the bowel was not firm; and he grew warm again. On the fortieth, without fever; the bowel was firm for no long time; without appetite; again he had slight fever.' Again: 'For if indeed it intermitted and they were relieved, it quickly relapsed again.' For relapsing is the opposite of being relieved. 'And the matters of the bowel,' he says, 'firming, and then again loosening.' For firming is the opposite of loosening. Next, setting out another patient, he says: 'On the eighth she was much deranged, and on the following days, and quickly was in her senses again.' And again next: 'On the twentieth she became slightly chilled, and quickly grew warm again.' And once more: 'On the twenty-seventh, without fever; the bowel was firm. Not long afterward, a strong pain in the right hip for a long time, and fevers again accompanied.' Then next: 'And on the following days she was voiceless, and then again was in her senses and conversed.' But why be long-winded, mentioning all of them, when they are ten thousand times ten thousand? So many are the instances from him of this very form of expression. Thus when he says 'comatose and then again sleepless', he manifestly sets coma in antithesis to sleeplessness. And indeed you can set a lapse into sleep in antithesis to sleeplessness, and so no other second meaning of 'coma' appears again. What about when he says: 'But there prevailed either continuous coma, not sleepy, or they were sleepless with pains'? For this form of expression too would be peculiar to Hippocrates: to remark on things that usually follow but now, contrary to reason, do not follow. For example, when he says: 'Now, burning fevers occurred in very few, and of the sick these suffered least. For there was no hemorrhage, except very slight and in a few, and no delirium.' And a little later: 'Nor do I know of anyone who died at that time from burning fever, nor of phrenitic conditions occurring at that time.' For this reason he similarly remarks that violent bleeding from the nostrils, the mind's being affected, and the incurring of acute dangers, none of these having happened at that time. And what is added, 'Nor do I know of phrenitic conditions occurring at that time', is said on the same principle. For burning fevers and phrenitis arise from the same constitutions and the same causes: of course they abound in the summer season, in hotter places, in the age of those in their prime, in hotter natures, and likewise in [hotter] regimens and occupations. And one would have expected phrenitic conditions also to abound, so that he remarks on what happened as contrary to reason: phrenitis did not occur at all, but burning fevers were many. In the same spirit this too has been said: 'The constitution of the burning fevers that occurred was as follows. At the beginning they were comatose, nauseated, shivering; fever not acute, nor were they very thirsty, nor delirious.' And a little later: 'For there was neither good hemorrhage, nor did any other of the usual abscessions occur as a crisis.' And how are these words said? 'Swellings beside the ears in many were on one side, and in most on both, in those without fever, on their feet; there were some who also became slightly warm; in all they subsided harmlessly, nor did they suppurate in anyone, as those from other causes [do].' For it is truly contrary to reason that nothing suppurated, and not at all usual. Then he adds: 'Their character was soft, large, diffuse, without inflammation'; for it is contrary to reason that the abscessions around the ears should occur in all without inflammation. So here too he again appears to apply 'coma' to the sleepy lapse, when he says: 'The coma was continuous, not sleepy'; for he remarks on it as something that ought to be sleepy, and as always occurring so, and then now, contrary to reason, not occurring so. And then, when in the same book, the third of the *Epidemics*, he says of Pythion: 'On the ninth, comatose, nauseated whenever he was roused': for clearly here too coma seems to denote a kind of lapse. But, they say, it is not possible to lapse and be sleepless at the same time. For so these marvelous commentators say, not knowing that there are two kinds of lapse, as the most esteemed physicians have written and the facts themselves testify. For common to both is that they cannot raise their eyes, but are at once weighed down and want to sleep; but peculiar to the one is that these sleep at once, deeply and for a long time, while the others are sleepless, tossing about, as one image comes upon another, stirring the mind and interrupting sleep, so that they always remain sleepless, yet are unable to get up and do what wakeful people do, but are in a more deficient state than if they were awake, and are weighed down and lapse, so that you will expect that, if you were to allow them, they would easily fall asleep; yet when this is allowed them, far from sleeping, they do not even keep the hope they had of going to sleep. Here, then, please understand coma as common to both, which we are of course accustomed to call lapse; but if you understand only the sleepy kind, you will err, for you will deprive the non-sleepy lapse of a name, though it needs the designation 'coma' no less than the other. So whether the lapse is sleepy or sleepless, it is his habit to call it coma; and the particulars are in no way in conflict with one another, but reasonably coma is found sometimes in slight states of sleeplessness, sometimes in sleep. For the lapse too is sometimes sleepy, sometimes sleepless, so that you cannot say of those who lapse that they are sleepless or that they are not; but they differ to this extent, that the majority of them sleep, while few of those in this condition remain sleepless; whence, although the affection belongs to both, it is nevertheless found to be much more proper to those who sleep. For this reason, then, he says: 'The coma was continuous, not sleepy', as it is usually sleepy. If, then, coma is common to both and more proper to sleep, it is reasonable that when he wishes to indicate the sleepy lapse, he says simply 'comatose'; but when, on the other hand, [he wishes to indicate] the sleepless [lapse], he says not simply, but with an addition, 'comatose, sleepless'. For he knows both things: that coma is more proper to sleep and more like its nature, and that there are times when it occurs along with sleeplessness. And if this is so, it is no wonder if it occurs not only in lethargics but also in phrenitics. The non-sleepy coma is not peculiar to these, but it occurs sometimes. For you will find many phrenitics neither getting up nor able to raise their eyes at all, but remaining in the same place like lethargics, so that the many uneducated physicians do not know what to call these, but are completely at a loss, and this affection seems to them foreign and nameless, and some suppose it a mixture of lethargy and phrenitis, and call it *typhomania* [stupefied madness]. And worst of all, some of those who pretend to be Hippocratics say this, although Hippocrates surely writes so clearly and plainly, not in a book of disputed authenticity, but in the third of the *Epidemics*, which is believed to be genuine if any other is: 'None of the phrenitics went raving mad, as in other cases, but they perished heavily in some other sluggish lapse.' For he has reported not only that a lapse sometimes occurs in cases of phrenitis, but also that it is often sluggish. And what is the sluggish [lapse]? You will first remember the division, if you are not going to misunderstand the present matters, when I called one lapse sleepy and the other sleepless, and [said] that the sleepy one is peculiar to lethargics and present in them throughout, while the other is neither peculiar to phrenitics nor present in them throughout.

The sleepy [lapse], then, so far as the present matter goes, occurs in lethargics; but the sleepless one, which comes upon phrenitics, I shall try to define, so that you may be able to discover the distinction stated by Hippocrates. For this man was not one of those who apply names idly, and 'sluggish' is not added to 'lapse' senselessly, nor does he speak, as Homer does, of 'liquid oil' and 'white milk', for the sake of no distinction, since all milk is white and all oil liquid; rather, in him each expression and every syllable signifies something. So, when discussing phrenitis, a thing useful for the present purpose to teach those who wish to learn his habitual usage, he sometimes writes thus, 'he talked nonsense'; sometimes thus, 'he was carried away'; sometimes again, 'he went off course'; and again, 'he was delirious'; and again, 'he was out of his mind'; and once more, 'he raved', and 'he went raving mad', and 'he did not comprehend', and 'he spoke amiss'. All these belong to those whose mind is impaired, all of whom you call delirious, but for Hippocrates it is not enough to name the genus alone: he has found a particular name for each degree of the form of delirium. For when he says 'A man, being warm, dined', he did not dare to call fever a heat so slight that one can dine in it. And again, wishing to indicate the severity of the fever, he says, 'Fire seized him.' I have spent time demonstrating the man's care over expressions, but now, as to those who already know and are persuaded, I shall come to the question at issue. The sleepless lapse has two forms. One is called sluggish, the one Hippocrates now mentions; the other uses the name of the genus. Common to both, and what most of all distinguishes them from the sleepy [lapse], is that they speak and babble things with no sense in them, and are very eager to get up, none of which is present in lethargic lapses. For neither do they say anything apart [...] and craftily, but are hard to rouse to sensation, nor are they easily woken by those who shout at them and prod them. But the phrenitic and sleepless coma is free of this dullness of sensation and difficulty of movement; for they get up easily on hearing a voice or any sound, and if you touch any part of the body, they at once raise their eyes and look toward the one touching them. And during the lapse itself they move a hand or a leg, or throw their whole body about without reason, and they leap up suddenly and deliriously, as in a spasm, and they do all this while also saying things that are not fitting, none of which lethargics with a lapse do, for they always lie motionless and voiceless, like those deeply asleep. Of those who lapse not in a sleepy way, some are so readily and so greatly mobile that they do not stop shouting loudly and moving some part violently; and if you rouse them or speak to them, they look at you in an unseemly way, become more deranged, and try to do harm, and are altogether most eager to listen, falling in no way short of those who are extremely delirious. Others, on the contrary, comprehend better when they get up, and do not move much, and are more delirious when you leave them to their coma. And it is chiefly by this that they can be distinguished from lethargic lapses. This, then, is the lapse called sluggish by Hippocrates. And since we have clearly learned that not only does lapsing happen to some phrenitics, but also doing so sluggishly (about this one might be especially at a loss), let us pass on to the remaining dispute, and if we find some solution to it, we shall then have the whole. The dispute is this. Hippocrates, mentioning in the *Prorrhetic* the sleepless comatose, is at a loss whether he will call them phrenitics or something else. It runs in order thus: 'Those who become comatose at the beginning, with pain of the head, loin, hypochondrium and neck, being sleepless: are they indeed phrenitics?' This passage is written in two ways, in some copies thus, in some without the 'are', 'indeed phrenitics?' But for now let us examine the first [reading]. Since there are two primary forms of coma, and one always occurs in lethargics, the other sometimes in phrenitics, Hippocrates is now at a loss whether those in this condition should be called phrenitics. Yet this seems, far from a difficulty, on the contrary easily discovered and ready to hand. For since there are two comas, and the sleepy one peculiar to lethargics cannot be meant here (for the added 'sleepless' does not allow this to be signified), he appears to be declaring of the remaining coma, '*ara ge* it is phrenitic.' How then is he at a loss? The word *ara*, he says, is inferential, not expressing doubt. But I might perhaps accept this, if it did not involve a barbarous interpretation, foreign to all Greek usage; but when neither the other Greeks nor Hippocrates are found using such a construction of propositions, how could I accept that the adverb *ara* is inferential? For before using premises in the argument and setting them before the conclusion, it is not possible to draw an inference. For example, so that what is said may be clear even to the less practised, '*ara ge*, is it day?' and '*ara ge*, will he come today?' contain an adverb expressing doubt. But if I wish to make a declaration about them in speech, [I do so] either speaking simply thus, without any demonstration, 'He will come today', or with demonstration thus: 'If the sun is above the earth, it is day'; 'If he walks, he therefore moves.' And when we declare something without demonstration, we have no need of the adverb *ara*, for the word is superfluous, and no one speaks thus, 'It is *ara* day', or thus, '*ara ge* it is day', when it is possible to say simply, 'It is day.' Nor can he use the *ara ge* in this way in a demonstration. For how could there be a demonstration, when every demonstration obtains one proposition from other premises? But he appears now to take no inferential premise for a demonstration. How then will the adverb *ara ge* become inferential and conclusive instead of expressing doubt? For with some [words] the adverb expressing doubt and the one called inferential and conclusive do not even hold the same position, but the one expressing doubt is always placed first, while the inferential and conclusive one is set between the noun and the predicate. For when in doubt we say, '*ara ge*, is it day?' but when inferring, thus: 'It is *ara* day.' Why then was it placed first here? It was placed first because it is not inferential. For it is not said thus, 'They are *ara* phrenitics', but simply, '*ara ge*, are they phrenitics?' with Hippocrates plainly at a loss, and not daring to declare firmly about them, as he evidently often does. One or two examples will suffice, so as not to spend longer on so clear a matter. In the first of the *Epidemics*, then, he says, 'After this all these became dysenteric. *Ara ge* because they passed watery urine? This must be considered.' Here the added 'must be considered' will not allow even the most shameless person to take the conjunction *ara* otherwise than as expressing doubt. And in the sixth of the *Epidemics*: 'The contraction after urination', he says, '[is] more in children; *ara ge* because they are warmer?' And in the *Prorrhetic* itself: 'In phrenitics a white evacuation is bad, as also in Archecrates. *Ara ge* does sluggishness also occur after these?' And again: 'In loss of voice, breathing like that of those choking, quick, is bad. *Ara ge* is such [a sign] also indicative of derangement?' If, then, one must put a head on the argument, and neither any other of the Greeks has used the conjunction *ara* in this way, nor Hippocrates himself, as I have now shown, one might, I think, blame those who explained it as not a conjunction expressing doubt.

And yet I know that I am making the argument harder for myself. For once the sleepy lapse has been distinguished from non-sleepy phrenitis, he would no longer seem to be properly at a loss and not firmly declaring such people to be phrenitics. But since I care less for difficulty in arguments than for truth, I admit that the conjunction expresses doubt, and I shall show the reason why Hippocrates did not dare to declare such people to be phrenitics, but is still at a loss. For the added 'at the beginning' holds the whole force of the statement, and most commentators pass over it, as though it had been added to no purpose. For something similar happens to those at the beginning of many diseases, such as can be seen happening in some who are drunk. When they are comatose, they both stumble and are heavy in the head, and cannot part their eyelids even if they force them; and yet because of this same heaviness they cannot sleep, but are restless, turning and throwing themselves about, and shifting now to one posture, now to another. For these things can often be seen happening in those who are drunk, when their head has been filled in drunkenness and then, by its heaviness, at once drags them down into coma and prevents sleep. So, in the same way, when an undigested excess has occupied the head, they are at once sleepless and comatose. And when this occurs at the beginning, sometimes it is well concocted, just as if such a thing had arisen from wine; and in this case neither lethargy nor phrenitis followed. But sometimes, having become acrid, it ended in phrenitis. And in many, again, the thinner part was evacuated, either concocted or dispersed, while the thicker remained, and so lethargy came on. When such a disease has advanced, such a condition, as we have shown, is already close to phrenitis; but, as those who introduce the affection mixed of lethargy and phrenitis suppose, it would seem to be more akin to that. Whether those in this condition should already be called phrenitics, or be expected to become so a little later, would be a matter for another inquiry, which does not help the present subject at all, and in any case through the 'are', which some add to '*ara* phrenitics' and some do not.
